messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan is an eighty-year-old widowed South Asian man who served for decades with the United States Coast Guard and who, in the final years of his active service, was at the helm of a rescue vessel when a navigational error during a fog-bound coastal operation caused the boat to strike a smaller craft. The collision was sudden and catastrophic. A junior crewman was pulled from the water with severe spinal injuries that left him partially paralysed, and though the official inquiry attributed the accident to conditions rather than negligence, Rajan never accepted that verdict. He remembered the particular quality of the light that morning — grey-green water, salt mist hanging low over the shoreline, the smell of diesel and kelp — and it was into that sensory world that his mind returned without warning for years afterward.

Rajan retired shortly after the incident and moved into a small house near the Massachusetts coast, where he had expected to spend his later years quietly. Instead, the environment that had defined his working life became a source of dread. Walking along the shoreline — something he had once done daily — now meant exposure to the same grey-green light, the same salt air, the same quality of open sky that surrounded the accident. When those natural cues registered, his body responded before his mind could intervene: his chest tightened, his attention narrowed, and the fragmented pieces of that morning began to surface unbidden. The memories did not arrive as a coherent narrative. They came in disconnected shards — the sound of impact, a flash of orange survival gear, a voice he could not place — that refused to assemble into a whole he could examine or put away. When he tried deliberately to reconstruct what had happened, the sequence dissolved; yet when a siren passed his window, or when a neighbour's scanner crackled with emergency traffic, the sensory world of the accident returned with full physical force, as though he were back on the water, the deck tilting beneath him. In those moments the reliving was total — not a recollection but a reinstatement, complete across every sense at once.

Because the memories arrived so violently and so incompletely, Rajan came to believe that the only way to survive them was to prevent their arrival. He told himself, with increasing conviction, that the accident had not been as serious as he remembered, or perhaps had not happened quite as he thought — a form of magical thinking that offered brief relief but left the underlying material untouched. He forced himself toward positive thoughts, rehearsing gratitude and forward-looking images, and when fragments surfaced anyway he pushed them down deliberately. These strategies quieted the surface without resolving anything beneath it, and over months he noticed that the memories seemed, if anything, more intrusive — as though suppression had kept them pressurised. There was a further cost he had not anticipated: because he had never stayed with a situation long enough to find out it was safe, his body had never received the evidence it needed, and the sense of threat remained as high and as immediate as it had been in the weeks after the accident — the avoidance and suppression had, in their own way, kept the danger feeling real and ongoing. The effort of managing his own mind also fed a darker conclusion: that a man who needed such constant mental labour to stay functional must have something fundamentally wrong with him. He had come to believe, with the quiet certainty of someone who has argued himself into a corner over years, that the accident had happened because of the kind of person he was — careless, arrogant, constitutionally unfit for the responsibility he had been given.

That appraisal of his own character sat at the centre of everything. Because he was certain he was defective, he was equally certain that danger was never far away — that his judgment could not be trusted, that unfamiliar environments held risks he would fail to assess correctly. And because he moved through the world already convinced of his own defectiveness, the environment seemed to conspire to confirm it — the grey-green light off the water, the smell of salt air, the distant sound of a foghorn all snagged his attention in a way they never had before the accident, each one registering not as neutral sensation but as evidence that the past was still present and still indicting him. He stopped travelling anywhere he had not been before. At the veterans' community centre where he occasionally attended lunch, he chose his seat with deliberate care, positioning himself with his back to the wall and a clear line to the exit. On days when the sense of threat ran highest — when his body was already primed and his vigilance already elevated — the memories were hardest to hold back; it was as though the adrenaline itself reached into the past and pulled the accident forward, so that the deck seemed to tilt beneath him again and the sound of the collision rang in his ears with fresh precision. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found that the world had become dense with signals he could not stop reading — a passing boat on the horizon, the particular angle of morning light over the water, the static crackle of any radio — each one catching in him like a hook, confirming what his nervous system already believed about the danger he carried with him. He had also, paradoxically, begun taking small physical risks — driving too fast on empty roads, neglecting prescribed medications — as though some part of him had decided that a man like him deserved whatever harm came his way. Talking about the future with his daughter, who visited on weekends, triggered the same cascade: any forward projection reminded him that the crewman he had injured was living a constrained life because of him, which brought the guilt flooding back and, with it, the fragments. His daughter noticed that he deflected every conversation about plans or hopes, and it was she who finally persuaded him to seek help. What Rajan most fears, sitting in the intake room, is that a clinician will confirm what he already believes about himself. What he most hopes, though he would not say so directly, is that someone will tell him he is wrong.
